row.question_original: I'm 70 and my eyesight seems fine. Should I get a screening vision test at my checkup?

replies:
It’s great that your eyesight feels fine—that’s a good sign! But even when everything seems normal, regular eye exams become especially important after age 65. Many common age-related eye conditions (like glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and diabetic eye disease) often have no early warning signs. By the time you notice a change in vision, some damage may already be irreversible.

A comprehensive **dilated eye exam** with an eye doctor (ophthalmologist or optometrist) can detect these problems early, when treatment is most effective. The American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends a full exam every 1–2 years for adults 65 and older, even without symptoms. A basic vision screening at a regular checkup—like reading a chart—is helpful but not thorough enough to rule out silent issues.

So yes, I’d definitely recommend adding a comprehensive eye exam to your healthcare routine, even now. It’s one of the simplest ways to protect your vision as you age.

Yes, I’m sure—and I appreciate you double-checking. It’s completely natural to question whether a test is necessary when your eyesight feels fine. Let me explain why the recommendation is so firm, even when you have no symptoms.

The key distinction is between a **screening vision test** (reading an eye chart at your regular checkup) and a **comprehensive dilated eye exam** with an eye doctor.

- A simple screening only checks how well you see at a distance. It can miss early signs of diseases that don’t affect central vision right away—like glaucoma, which first steals peripheral vision, or early macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, which can begin without any vision change.
- A comprehensive exam includes dilating your pupils so the doctor can directly view your optic nerve, retina, and blood vessels. This is how they detect these “silent” conditions before you’re aware of them.

The evidence is strong: major organizations like the **American Academy of Ophthalmology** and the **American Optometric Association** specifically recommend a comprehensive eye exam every 1–2 years for all adults 65 and older, regardless of symptoms. This isn’t because something is necessarily wrong—it’s because many age-related eye diseases are treatable if caught soon enough, and the only way to catch them early is to look inside the eye.

So while a basic vision check can be a good start, it’s not enough to confirm that your eyes are truly healthy. Think of it this way: “Eyes feel fine” is a great report, but it’s not the same as “eyes have been thoroughly examined.” You’re doing exactly the right thing by asking, and a comprehensive exam at this stage is a wise precaution.

DO IT

Yes, you should get a comprehensive dilated eye exam, not just a basic vision screening. Because you’re 70, it’s the only way to catch silent, age-related eye diseases early—before they cause permanent damage.
